title: Neutralisation Enthalpy: Strong vs Weak Compared
subtitle: Why a weak acid releases less heat
subject: Chemistry
syllabusDotPoints: conduct a practical investigation to measure the enthalpy of neutralisation (ACSCH093)
inquiryQuestion: What is an acid and what is a base?
lessonIntent: Students can explain why weak acids and bases give a less exothermic neutralisation and quantify the ionisation enthalpy from calorimetry data.
examSkill: Rank ΔHn by sign, explain the endothermic ionisation step at the molecular level, and compute ΔH(ionisation) = ΔHn(weak + NaOH) − ΔHn(HCl + NaOH).

introVoiceover.text: Welcome to HSC Science. This is HSC Chemistry. Today, comparing the neutralisation enthalpy of strong and weak acids. Let's get into it.

scenes.caption: Neutralisation Enthalpy: Strong vs Weak Compared (Year 12 Chemistry, Module 6, Lesson 10)

scenes.heading: Comparing two temperature rises
scenes.body: Matched neutralisation experiments can release different amounts of heat.
scenes.callout: Use a measured baseline and account for all assumptions.
scenes.caption: Use a measured baseline and account for all assumptions.

voiceover.text: OK, compare a strong acid and a weak acid reacting with the same strong base under matched conditions. Both can neutralise, yet their temperature rises may differ. For a dilute strong acid with a strong base, the enthalpy is commonly about minus fifty seven kilojoules per mole of water. Acetic acid can give a less negative result because ionisation contributes to the overall energy change. Today we calculate that difference and practise interpreting it carefully. A heat measurement gives an enthalpy change. Acid strength is described by an equilibrium constant, so it cannot be ranked from the heat difference alone.

scenes.heading: A reference, not a universal limit
scenes.body: Dilute strong-acid/strong-base neutralisation is commonly about −57 kJ mol⁻¹ of water.

bullets.text: Dilute strong acid + strong base: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.
About −57 kJ mol⁻¹ is a useful matched-condition reference.
Other reaction and dilution enthalpies can affect measured values.

scenes.secondary: −57 kJ mol⁻¹ is an approximate reference for dilute strong acid + strong base, not an absolute lower bound.
scenes.callout: Use the same conditions when comparing enthalpies.
scenes.caption: Use the same conditions when comparing enthalpies.

voiceover.text: For a dilute strong acid and a strong base, the main net ionic reaction is hydrogen ions plus hydroxide ions forming water. Under comparable conditions its enthalpy is commonly near minus fifty seven kilojoules per mole of water. This is a useful reference, not an absolute maximum for every neutralisation experiment. Concentration, dilution, temperature and the reacting species can affect a measured value. A result more negative than the reference deserves investigation, but it is not automatically impossible. Remember that a more negative enthalpy means more heat released per mole, so minus fifty two is less exothermic than minus fifty seven.

scenes.heading: Ionisation contributes to the heat balance
scenes.body: Acetic acid ionises as H⁺ is consumed by OH⁻; its ionisation contributes to the net enthalpy.

bullets.text: CH₃COOH ⇌ H⁺ + CH₃COO⁻; removal of H⁺ promotes further ionisation.
In this example the ionisation contribution is endothermic.
Hess law adds ionisation and neutralisation enthalpies under matched conditions.

scenes.secondary: For this acetic-acid example, an endothermic ionisation contribution reduces the heat released. Heat loss and dilution must also be considered.
scenes.callout: A positive ionisation contribution makes this example less exothermic.
scenes.caption: A positive ionisation contribution makes this example less exothermic.

voiceover.text: For acetic acid with sodium hydroxide, removal of hydrogen ions draws further acetic acid into ionisation. We can represent the overall reaction as ionisation of the acid followed by neutralisation of the hydrogen ions. Enthalpy changes add by Hess law. In an example where ionisation is endothermic, that contribution makes the overall reaction less exothermic than the matched strong-acid baseline. This is an energy balance, not proof that the weak acid fails to neutralise. In a real experiment we must also consider heat loss and dilution. The difference estimates the ionisation contribution only when those other effects are controlled or accounted for.

scenes.heading: Enthalpy and strength are different quantities

bullets.text: Neutralisation enthalpy: reaction enthalpy per mole of water formed.
Ionisation enthalpy: the enthalpy change for ionisation in solution.
Acid strength: Ka, governed by ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°.
Matched difference: ΔHn(acid + NaOH) − ΔHn(reference + NaOH).

scenes.callout: Ka depends on Gibbs energy, including entropy, not on enthalpy alone.
scenes.caption: Ka depends on Gibbs energy, including entropy, not on enthalpy alone.

voiceover.text: The enthalpy of neutralisation is the reaction enthalpy per mole of water formed for the acid and base considered here. Ionisation enthalpy is the enthalpy change when an acid ionises in solution, including interactions with the solvent. Acid strength is described by K a. The standard Gibbs energy change is minus R T natural log K a, and Gibbs energy includes both enthalpy and entropy. Therefore a bigger positive ionisation enthalpy does not by itself prove a smaller K a. In matched experiments the weak-acid neutralisation enthalpy minus the strong-acid baseline estimates an ionisation contribution. Its sign must come from the data; it is not universally positive.

scenes.heading: Compare measured combinations
scenes.body: These are illustrative enthalpy magnitudes under specified, matched conditions.

bullets.text: These bars show an illustrative data set under matched conditions.
Different acids and bases have different reaction enthalpies.
Heat magnitudes alone do not establish a Ka ranking.

scenes.secondary: The values shown are illustrative data, not universal constants. Write the net ionic reaction for each combination.
scenes.callout: Use data for each reaction; do not infer a universal strength ranking.
scenes.caption: Use data for each reaction; do not infer a universal strength ranking.

voiceover.text: An illustrative data set might give enthalpy magnitudes of fifty seven for hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide, fifty five for acetic acid with sodium hydroxide, fifty two for hydrochloric acid with ammonia, and forty nine for acetic acid with ammonia. These bars illustrate this particular data set, not a universal order for all acids and bases. Different species have different reaction and solvation enthalpies. Also, when ammonia accepts a proton, the net ionic equation is not simply hydrogen ions plus hydroxide forming water. Compare matched experiments and write the relevant reaction before interpreting the heat. Do not treat every weak partner as paying the same compulsory endothermic toll.

scenes.heading: Comparing two ΔHn
scenes.question: Both 50.0 mL + 50.0 mL at 1.00 mol L⁻¹. HCl+NaOH: 21.0→27.8 °C. CH₃COOH+NaOH: 21.0→27.2 °C. Find each ΔHn.
scenes.coachNote: Assume matched heat losses, density 1.00 g mL⁻¹ and c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.
steps: Under the stated assumptions: apparent ionisation contribution = −51.8 − (−56.8) = +5.0 kJ mol⁻¹.
scenes.caption: Comparing two ΔHn

voiceover.text: For the supplied measurements, both experiments mix fifty millilitres of acid and fifty millilitres of base at one molar. Assume density one gram per millilitre, specific heat capacity four point one eight, and negligible other heat terms. The total mass is one hundred grams and nought point zero five moles of water form. Hydrochloric acid gives a temperature rise of six point eight degrees, so q is two point eight four two kilojoules and the reaction enthalpy is minus fifty six point eight kilojoules per mole. Acetic acid gives a rise of six point two, so q is two point five nine two and the enthalpy is minus fifty one point eight. Subtract the matched baseline to get a difference of positive five point zero kilojoules per mole. Under our assumptions this estimates an ionisation contribution for these supplied measurements. It is not a universal tabulated value for acetic acid.

scenes.heading: Interpreting three unknowns
scenes.question: Mix 50.0 mL of each 1.00 mol L⁻¹ monoprotic acid X, Y, Z separately with 50.0 mL of 1.00 mol L⁻¹ NaOH. All start at 20.0 °C; maxima are X 26.6, Y 26.8, Z 25.9 °C. Assume matched heat losses, density 1.00 g mL⁻¹ and c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹. Compare ΔHn and say whether Ka can be ranked.
scenes.coachNote: Compare measured ΔHn; do not infer Ka from heat alone.
steps: Relative to Y: X is +1.6 and Z is +7.5 kJ mol⁻¹ less exothermic.
Answer: Z releases less heat per mole; Ka cannot be ranked from ΔHn alone.
scenes.caption: Heat data alone cannot establish the Ka ranking.

voiceover.text: Now compare three unknowns. Each experiment mixes fifty millilitres of one molar acid with fifty millilitres of one molar sodium hydroxide. Assume monoprotic acids, complete neutralisation, matched heat losses and the same density and specific heat capacity. X rises by six point six degrees, giving minus fifty five point two kilojoules per mole. Y rises by six point eight, giving minus fifty six point eight. Z rises by five point nine, giving minus forty nine point three. Relative to Y, the differences are positive one point six for X and positive seven point five for Z. Z is less exothermic in these experiments. These results can suggest different ionisation contributions, but they cannot establish which acid has the smaller K a. To rank strength, use an equilibrium measurement such as pH at a known concentration.

scenes.callout: Heat data alone cannot establish the Ka ranking.

scenes.heading: Three interpretation traps
scenes.body: A smaller ΔT can reflect reaction enthalpy or experimental heat loss.
scenes.secondary: −57 is a reference, not a universal bound. Ka depends on Gibbs energy, including entropy, so calorimetry alone cannot rank strength.
scenes.callout: A larger heat difference does not by itself mean a weaker acid.
scenes.caption: A larger heat difference does not by itself mean a weaker acid.

voiceover.text: Three traps. First, assuming a smaller temperature rise proves an incomplete reaction. It may reflect a different enthalpy, heat loss, or other experimental effects. Second, calling minus fifty seven an absolute limit for all acids and bases. It is a useful dilute strong-acid and strong-base reference under comparable conditions. Third, ranking acid strength from the enthalpy difference alone. K a depends on Gibbs energy, including entropy, so calorimetry by itself does not give that ranking. State your experimental assumptions, compare like with like, and keep energy measurements separate from equilibrium measurements.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: A matched strong-acid/NaOH reference gives ΔHn = −57 kJ mol⁻¹; an unknown monoprotic acid/NaOH gives −43. Assume heat loss and dilution effects are controlled. Find the apparent extra enthalpy contribution. Can this alone rank Ka?
answerSteps: Under the assumptions, this is an apparent endothermic contribution relative to the reference.
It is consistent with an ionisation contribution after other heat terms are accounted for.
Ka depends on ΔG°, including entropy, so the heat difference alone cannot rank acid strength.
scenes.caption: Quick check

voiceover.text: The matched strong-acid reference is minus fifty seven kilojoules per mole, while an unknown acid with sodium hydroxide gives minus forty three. Under the stated assumptions, subtracting the reference gives positive fourteen kilojoules per mole. That is an apparent endothermic contribution relative to the baseline. It is consistent with endothermic ionisation, but only after heat loss, dilution and other effects have been controlled. We cannot conclude that the acid is weaker than acetic acid from this number alone. For that comparison we need equilibrium data, such as K a derived from pH at a known concentration.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: About −57 kJ mol⁻¹ is a dilute strong-acid/strong-base reference, not a universal bound.
Ionisation and solvation can contribute to the measured reaction enthalpy.
Use Hess law with stated reactions and matched conditions.
Account for heat loss, dilution and the limiting amount that reacts.
Enthalpy alone cannot rank Ka: Gibbs energy also includes entropy.
scenes.finalPrompt: Comparing ΔHn? Remember more negative means more exothermic.
scenes.caption: Lock it in

voiceover.text: Keep five ideas. Use about minus fifty seven as a matched dilute strong-acid and strong-base reference, not a universal bound. Ionisation and solvation contribute to the heat of other reactions. Apply Hess law only with clearly stated reactions and comparable conditions. Check heat loss, dilution and the amount that actually reacts before interpreting a difference. Finally, enthalpy alone does not rank acid strength, because K a depends on Gibbs energy, including entropy. Calculate the heat carefully, state what the data support, and use equilibrium measurements when the question asks about strength.
